title: Latitudinal Phylogenetic and Diversity Gradients Are Explained by a Tropical‐Temperate Transitional Bioregion
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

To investigate how large-scale ecological and evolutionary processes shape biodiversity patterns, with a focus on understanding the origins of latitudinal phylogenetic and diversity gradients. We emphasize the importance of accurately delineating bioregions to reveal the underlying evolutionary structure of biodiversity.

Location

Global, with emphasis on transitions between tropical and temperate bioregions.

Time Period

Contemporary distributions, analysed in the context of deep evolutionary histories.

Major Taxa Studied

Woody angiosperm tree species.

Methods

We compiled a comprehensive dataset of global tree species distributions and phylogenetic relationships. Using a data-driven clustering approach, we delineated phyloregions: bioregions based on shared evolutionary history. We further applied simulation models to test whether the presence of transitional regions influences the emergence of latitudinal gradients.

Results

We identified a previously unrecognized transitional zone between tropical and temperate bioregions, termed the “bridge” phyloregion. This phyloregion is characterized by a distinct evolutionary composition and a weaker association with climatic and environmental parameters compared with adjacent phyloregions. Simulation models demonstrate that the latitudinal diversity and phylogenetic gradients are much more likely to emerge when such a transitional phyloregion exists. This finding supports the interpretation of the bridge phyloregion as a stepping-stone facilitating colonization of species between contrasting climatic zones.

Main Conclusions

Our findings reveal that accurate delineation of evolutionary bioregions (phyloregions) uncovers previously hidden structures, including a bridge phyloregion with fundamental evolutionary roles. Recognizing these cryptic phyloregions provides new insights into the processes leading to large-scale patterning of biodiversity.
